note: Free, no-login pages for each topic, checked by hand. Links and our own one-line summaries only: nothing is copied from them. Types: notes, syllabus, interactive. No videos.

t1.title: Structure of the atom
t1.why: A short, clear page on the nucleus, the shells and the charge and mass of each particle.
t1.caution: Some BBC videos may not play outside the UK. The written notes always work.

t1.title: Atomic number and mass number
t1.why: Shows how to get protons, neutrons and electrons from the two numbers, with a question to try.
t1.caution: It says atomic number and mass number. Your syllabus calls them proton number and nucleon number.

t1.title: O-Level Chemistry 6092 syllabus, section 2.2 Atomic Structure
t1.why: The official list of what you must be able to do for this topic, so you know exactly what is asked.

t1.title: Build an Atom
t1.publisher: PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder
t1.why: Drag protons, neutrons and electrons into an atom and watch the element, charge and mass change.

t2.title: Electronic structure
t2.why: Explains the 2, 8, 8 filling rule and how shells link to the Period and Group.
t2.caution: The BBC writes 2,8,1 with commas. In Singapore exams write it with dots: 2.8.1.

t2.title: O-Level Chemistry 6092 syllabus, section 2.2 Atomic Structure
t2.why: Confirms you only need electrons in shells: s, p, d and f are not required.

t2.title: Build an Atom
t2.publisher: PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder
t2.why: Add electrons one at a time and see the first shell fill with 2 before the second shell starts.
t2.caution: It only goes up to neon, so you see two shells, not three.

t3.title: Isotopes
t3.why: Same protons, different neutrons, explained with the three isotopes of hydrogen.
t3.caution: Some BBC videos may not play outside the UK. The written notes always work.

t3.title: Calculating relative atomic mass
t3.why: Works through chlorine to show why its relative atomic mass is 35.5 and not a whole number.

t3.title: Isotopes and Atomic Mass
t3.publisher: PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder
t3.why: Add neutrons to make different isotopes, then mix them and watch the average mass move.

t3.title: O-Level Chemistry 6092 syllabus, section 2.2 Atomic Structure
t3.why: Shows that you need to define isotopes and use nuclide notation for them.

t4.title: Ionic bonding
t4.why: Metal atoms give electrons to non-metal atoms, with examples like sodium chloride and magnesium oxide.

t4.title: Ionic (electrovalent) bonding
t4.why: A calm, careful explanation of why atoms lose or gain electrons, worked through for NaCl, MgO and CaCl₂.
t4.caution: Read the simple first part only. The page then goes on to A-level ideas you do not need.

t4.title: O-Level Chemistry 6092 syllabus, section 3.1 Ionic Bonding
t4.why: Lists the examples you are expected to draw, such as NaCl and MgCl₂.

t5.title: Covalent bonding
t5.why: How non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons, and how to work out how many bonds each atom makes.

t5.title: Dot and cross models
t5.why: Dot-and-cross pictures of common molecules showing outer shells only, the way exams want them.

t5.title: O-Level Chemistry 6092 syllabus, section 3.2 Covalent Bonding
t5.why: Names the molecules you should be able to draw: H₂, O₂, H₂O, CH₄ and CO₂.

t6.title: Giant ionic structures
t6.why: Why the ionic lattice gives high melting points and conducts only when molten or dissolved.
t6.caution: Later pages in this guide cover diamond, graphite and metals. Those are Pure Chemistry extras, not this topic.

t6.title: Properties of simple molecular substances
t6.why: Why small molecules melt and boil easily and do not conduct electricity.

t6.title: Ionic structures
t6.why: Links the sodium chloride lattice to its melting point, brittleness and conductivity, step by step.
t6.caution: The part on caesium chloride goes beyond O-level. You can skip it.

t6.title: O-Level Chemistry 6092 syllabus, section 3.4 Structure and Properties of Materials
t6.why: Shows you must use structure and bonding to explain properties, and the other way round.
